title: All the taints
hook: seven ways to deal with the taints: seeing, restraining, using, enduring, avoiding, removing, developing (MN 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: mannati, building a self-story out of anything, even nibbana. Your line: not pleased, yet.

An old wooden boat has a slow leak. Water seeps in at the seams; you can bail all day and still, by evening, your ankles are wet. One seam needs caulking. Another only leaks when you scrape the rocks, so you steer around them. A third you just live with, and bail. Different leaks, different fixes, and the mistake is using one fix for all of them. The Buddha had a word for what leaks in a mind, and seven ways to deal with it.
screen: `A BOAT WITH A SLOW LEAK.` → `DIFFERENT SEAMS, DIFFERENT FIXES.` → `SEVEN WAYS.`

segments.voice: The word is asava, from a root meaning to flow. Translators reach for taints, cankers, outflows. In MN 2, the Sabbasava, the Buddha names three: the taint of sense desire, the taint of being, the craving to exist and keep existing, and the taint of ignorance. Then, instead of one remedy, he gives seven. Some taints are abandoned by seeing: understanding clearly, which comes tomorrow. Some by restraining: guarding the eye and the ear. Some by using: food, clothing, shelter and medicine used for what they're for, not for show or intoxication. Some by enduring: cold and heat, hunger and thirst, hurtful words and pain, borne patiently. Some by avoiding: a wild elephant, a thorny path, a cliff edge, and, right alongside them, bad company. Some by removing: when a thought of greed, ill will or cruelty comes, not putting up with it, but dispelling it. And some by developing: the seven factors of awakening. What makes this practical is that it refuses to use one tool for every job. You don't endure a charging elephant; you step out of its way. You can't avoid hunger forever; some of it you endure. You don't restrain your way out of confusion; you look more clearly. Seven ways, like a ring of keys: the skill is knowing which door you're standing at.
screen: `ASAVA — WHAT FLOWS.` · `THREE TAINTS.` · `SEVEN WAYS, NOT ONE.` · `THE RIGHT KEY FOR THE DOOR.` · then, large: `SEVEN WAYS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that drains you, a habit, a craving, an irritation that keeps coming back, and hold it up to the seven ways, one per breath: seeing, restraining, using, enduring, avoiding, removing, developing. One of them will fit. Rest with the breath, holding that choice lightly.
Asava. The taints: what flows in the mind and keeps it bound. Sense desire, the craving to be, and ignorance.
Your line: seven ways. The right tool depends on the leak. Day four hundred three.

howItsDone: Theravada monastics reflect on the four requisites, robes, food, shelter and medicine, as MN 2 describes, often by reciting a short reflection before using them; the destruction of the taints is a traditional description of awakening.

what a scholar hears: āsava also names a fermented drink, which is why some early translators chose 'intoxicants'; the destruction of the āsavas is a standard phrase for awakening.

chat.says: If something keeps dragging you down, is there one best way to fight it?
options: MN 2 gives seven ways, like seeing, enduring or avoiding; use the one that fits.
Yes, just willpower: push every bad habit down the same way, every time.
No, the Buddha says simply accept whatever drags you, and never act on it.
chat.meaning: MN 2 gives seven ways with the taints: seeing, restraining, using, enduring, avoiding, removing and developing. Each fits a different job.
